notes:
# Proverbs 24: Verse-by-Verse Research Notes

**Coverage:** I fully read three pages: Guzik (Enduring Word), Gill and the Pulpit Commentary. The Guzik and Pulpit pages were cut off, Guzik partway through v. 19 and Pulpit at v. 17, so my notes on the later verses come from search-result excerpts. My research found nothing on bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or the prosperity / word of faith / hyper-grace debate, so those parts are left out except where noted. The tradition labels (for example "Methodist Clarke") are my own shorthand.

---

**v. 1:** Guzik says envying evil people is a common temptation when they seem to do well, and that envy can lead to wanting their company. He cites Kidner: the cure for envy is to take "the long view." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/
- Gill reads "evil men" as the gluttons and drunkards of ch. 23. He says not to envy their success, because ruin follows, and adds: if you wouldn't want to be with them in hell, don't want to be with them now. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html
- Pulpit: Their company is pollution, and association with them makes you a partner in their sinful doings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-24.html

**v. 2:** Pulpit notes that the Latin Vulgate's word means violence of every kind, such as robbery and murder. It says their lips talk of mischief; utter lies and slanders which may injure other people or bring themselves profit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-24.html
- Gill: their schemes against others often come back on themselves. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 3:** Guzik applies the verse both to building an actual house and to the moral and spiritual values of a home. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/
- Pulpit: a family is kept up and prospers through prudence, honesty and the fear of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Gill adds a spiritual reading: Christ, who is Wisdom, builds the church. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 4:** Pulpit: Material prosperity, copious store of necessaries, and wealth, follow on wisdom; how much more do spiritual blessings attend the fear of God! https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Ellicott: Not only earthly wealth, but the "true riches" (Luke 16:11), the knowledge and love of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm
- Guzik says the riches are spiritual and often material too. He quotes Garrett, who says the jewels are a loving family and a sense of security. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/
- These sources weigh material against spiritual riches differently. None of them discusses prosperity teaching.

**v. 5:** Pulpit: the wise man is strong even if his body is weak, because he is wise in counsel and trusts God. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "a wise man is better than a strong man." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Gill: the wise person is strong "in Christ," not in himself. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 6:** Guzik: wisdom is not a solo effort; it draws on the advice of others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/
- Ellicott: In the great spiritual fight also (Ephesians 6:12) we need wise counsel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm
- Gill: kings should first ask whether a war is just, and above all ask God's advice. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 7:** Ellicott: the fool has been too self-willed to learn; so while others express their opinions when the business or justice of his city is being transacted... he has to remain sheepishly silent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm
- Pulpit reports that Delitzsch reads "too high" as "precious things": to the fool, wisdom looks like an expensive extra that isn't worth the effort. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Guzik quotes Poole: the fool calls wisdom impossible because he won't put in the work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/

**v. 8:** Pulpit: literally a "lord of mischief." His apparent cleverness is not wisdom, and he will soon be exposed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Gill: everyone is prone to evil, but this man sits down and invents new sins. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 9:** Ellicott translates it as Sin is the contrivance (plotting) of self-will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm
- Gill: The thought of sin is sin even before it becomes action, and so needs pardon. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html
- Pulpit: the book of Proverbs keeps linking sin with folly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm

**v. 10:** Pulpit points out a Hebrew wordplay (tsarah, "adversity," and tsar, "small"). It renders it "If thou faint in time of straitness, straitened is thy strength." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Guzik: hard times don't make your strength small; they show that it is small. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/
- Gill mentions other readings that link the verse to vv. 7 or 11. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 11:** Pulpit says the sentence is a command, not a condition. It quotes Cheyne: the victims of a miscarriage of justice are being led off to execution, and the student of wisdom is told to try to save them. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/24-11.htm
- Clarke: if you see innocent people about to be killed, plead for them, or you share the guilt for their blood. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ncv/proverbs/24-11.html
- Gill extends the verse to people drawn into sin or heresy and in danger of eternal death. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html
- Guzik quotes Garrett, who allows both a literal and a spiritual reading and gives the Holocaust as a modern example. Guzik himself points to Esther. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/
- A modern application in the BibleHub study notes includes Speak for unborn children or other vulnerable people (Psalm 82:4). https://biblehub.com/proverbs/24-11.htm

**v. 12:** Ellicott ties the excuse to Cain's "Am I my brother's keeper?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm
- Pulpit: Jerome's Latin makes the excuse "I don't have the strength," and the Septuagint makes it "I don't know the man." Such a person passes by like the priest and Levite in the Good Samaritan story. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Guzik quotes Waltke: if you turn a blind eye to victims, God may turn a blind eye to you. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/

**v. 13:** Pulpit: honey was eaten as food and used as medicine, and was a staple for children, which made it a picture of pure wisdom (compare Psalm 19:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Gill: the point is less the honey itself than the wisdom it stands for. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 14:** Pulpit: the teacher wants his student to enjoy wisdom, not just find it useful. The word translated "reward" literally means "future." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Guzik quotes Garrett: right living is also the road to real pleasure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/
- Gill reads the wisdom as knowing Christ, which is the beginning of eternal life. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 15:** Pulpit: "O wicked man" is addressed directly to him. The Vulgate reads "seek not impiety in the house of the righteous," which Pulpit takes as a warning not to dress up your plotting as God's punishment of a good man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm

**v. 16: the main point where interpreters differ**
- **Falling into trouble, not sin:** Ellicott says it means falls into trouble (not sin, as is often supposed). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm Barnes agrees: The point of the teaching is not the liability of good men to err, but God's providential care over them. The Cambridge Bible adds that the Hebrew word is never used of moral lapse, but into trouble or calamity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/24-16.htm
- **The Methodist Clarke** quotes Holden, who complains that some expound it by the just man often relapsing into sin, and recovering from it; nay, it has even been adduced to prove the doctrine of the final perseverance of the elect. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/proverbs/24-17.html
- **The Calvinist Baptist Gill** keeps both senses but prefers "trouble" from the context. He says the sin reading has been anciently received, and not to be rejected. A truly just man may fall into gross sin but not totally and finally, so as to perish; he rises by renewed repentance. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/proverbs/24-16.html
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** reads the verse mainly as suffering. Seven stands for what can feel like a total loss, and the verse looks ahead to the final resurrection. It also quotes Matthew Henry applying it to "sins of infirmity" followed by repentance. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/fall-and-rise-righteous
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel):** many insist on "trouble," but he sees no good reason it can't include both. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/
- **Older Catholic usage:** Pulpit says preachers have often used the verse to teach that a good man may fall into venial or more serious sins, but he never loses his love of God. It adds that the words "in die" ("a day") are often added and appear in some manuscripts but are not in the original. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/24-16.htm Wycliffe's 1395 Bible has "seven times in the day." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/proverbs/24-16.html (I found no Catholic sites on this.)
- GotQuestions: seven may simply mean "often," or completeness. https://www.gotquestions.org/righteous-man-falls-seven-times.html

**v. 17:** Pulpit: the verse is close to "Love your enemies." It applies to private enemies; public enemies' defeats were often celebrated. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/24-17.htm
- Gill makes the same private/public distinction and says even secret gladness is forbidden. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/csb/proverbs/24-17.html
- Poole: this shows loving enemies is commanded in the Old Testament as well as the New. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/24-17.htm

**v. 18:** The motive given here has troubled commentators.
- Keil & Delitzsch argue the point is not to let the enemy suffer longer, but to avoid God's displeasure at your gloating. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/24-17.htm
- Chuck Smith calls it not too good a motivation. Coffman, quoting the International Critical Commentary, says God may care more about punishing his own disobedient follower. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/24-17.html
- Clarke: God may turn his wrath away from the enemy and pour it out on thee. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/proverbs/24-17.html
- Guzik quotes Ross: if we want God to keep up his anger, we had better not gloat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/

**v. 19:** Pulpit: the verb means "to burn," so the sense is "Be not enraged on account of evildoers." That anger would arise on account of the apparent inequitable distribution of blessings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-24.html
- Guzik likewise says "fret" is too mild. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-24/

**v. 20:** Ellicott: "no reward" is literally "no future," the same word as in v. 14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm

**v. 21:** Pulpit: The king is God's vicegerent and representative, and therefore to be honoured and obeyed. The Hebrew shonim is debated: it may mean "innovators" or, following Delitzsch, "those who are otherwise disposed" toward God and the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Matthew Henry: There may be cause to change for the better, but have nothing to do with them that are given change. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/24-17.htm

**v. 22:** Nothing found.

**v. 23:** Pulpit: the first line introduces a new collection. Calling partiality "not good" is an understatement meaning it is very sinful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
- Gill thinks these are probably still Solomon's words. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-24.html

**v. 24:** Pulpit: the picture is a judge acquitting a guilty person. Some translate the verb "the peoples shall stab him." In this case the vox populi is vox Dei (the voice of the people is the voice of God). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-24.html
- Pulpit's sermon notes: when justice fails, the very nerve of public right is unstrung. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/24.htm

**v. 25:** Nothing beyond Pulpit's remark that vv. 24–25 develop v. 23. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm

**v. 26:** Ellicott: He kisseth the lips that giveth right answers. His words are as pleasant as if he had kissed the inquirer's lips. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm

**v. 27:** Ellicott: Method in work is here advised; first till the ground, and then build the house which will be maintained by the produce of the field. He applies it spiritually to knowing our real duties. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm
- Matthew Henry: We must prefer necessaries before conveniences, and not go in debt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/24-17.htm

**v. 28:** Pulpit: "without cause" means gratuitously. Persons are not to put themselves forward to give testimony to a neighbour's discredit, either officiously as busybodies, or maliciously as slanderers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-24.html
- Ellicott: don't mention a neighbour's faults without good reason. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm

**v. 29:** Ellicott calls it A wonderful anticipation this of New Testament teaching, very different from the spirit of Leviticus 24:19-20. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm
- Pulpit: The lex talionis should not be applied to private wrongs. (lex talionis is the "eye for an eye" law.) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm

**vv. 30–32:** Ellicott sees a spiritual meaning: don't let the weeds of bad habits grow in the soul through laziness, or lose God's protecting "wall" through neglecting prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/24.htm
- Pulpit's sermon notes: the neglected field shows the sluggard's soul, and there is still time to restore it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/24.htm

**vv. 33–34:** Pulpit: these verses nearly repeat Proverbs 6:10–11, perhaps added by a later editor. Verse 33 is the sluggard's own words; v. 34 is the result. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/24.htm
